extracted.intended_audience: stand-up comedians, comedy writers, and critics focused on craft and recorded specials
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for writing, performing, and recording stand-up material—with emphasis on hour-long specials, persona, room choice (alt vs mainstream), and adapting material for recorded media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis-driven hour vs string of bits
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the hour have a thesis, or just bits? The expectation has shifted from 'string of bits' to 'essayistic argument.' Splitsider argued the best new specials had a THESIS, not just material; the thesis-driven hour creates emotional architecture, while the bit-driven hour creates whiplash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the set is organized around a clear, sustained idea (thesis) that yields emotional and narrative payoff. Anti-patterns: disconnected bits that only aim for micro-laughs without contributing to an overarching argument or arc. Consider pacing, callbacks, and how early material foreshadows later payoff as evidence of a thesis-driven structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persona authenticity (persona as constructed instrument)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comedian's persona is a constructed instrument. The 'authentic' comedian is one whose persona is closely fitted to their actual self; the 'fake' comedian is one whose persona contradicts the off-stage person. Audiences detect the gap, even when they can't articulate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the fit between onstage persona and known/implicit offstage identity: consistency, believability, and whether the persona enables rather than obstructs jokes. Guidance: treat persona as a tool—shape it to amplify strengths and truthful observation. Anti-patterns: contrived personas that rely on obvious artifice or that clash with offstage signals (interviews, social media), which can erode audience trust and laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'comedians as therapists' framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Splitsider repeatedly criticized the framing of comedians as societal therapists: the comic's job is comedy; therapy is a side effect of GOOD comedy. Comics who lean into the therapist framing usually become less funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize humor over therapeutic messaging. Evaluate whether material uses self-exposure or 'helpful' messaging at the expense of punch and comic craft. Anti-patterns: sets that hinge on earnest confessions presented as therapeutic interventions or moral instruction rather than engineered for comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alt comedy as a permission structure & audience expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Alt comedy is not a style; it's a permission structure. Audiences in alt rooms forgive experimentation and demand originality; audiences in mainstream rooms forgive familiarity and demand reliability. Comics develop in alt rooms, monetize in mainstream rooms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use room-type to set goals: experiment and risk in alt rooms to refine voice; use mainstream rooms when reliability and broad appeal are the priority. Evaluate whether material, risk level, and delivery fit the room's expectations. Anti-patterns: treating 'alt' as a fixed style rather than a development space; expecting alt-level experimentation to translate unchanged to mainstream audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimize material for recorded medium
rubrics_metrics.description: The medium changes the material. A bit that kills live can flatten on tape. Pros write WITH the recorded medium in mind for hours intended for streaming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether timing, pacing, visual staging, and the structure of jokes account for cameras and the absence/presence of a live audience in playback. Guidance includes testing how bits edit, whether tags survive close-ups, and whether quieter, nuance-driven moments translate to a recorded special. Anti-patterns: relying on immediate live-room energy or crowd work as the primary engine of laughs without alternate strategies for a recording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimize for funny first, message second
rubrics_metrics.description: Are you optimizing for funny first, message second? Splitsider emphasizes comedy should prioritize humor; message or social insight should be subordinate to what makes the audience laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether jokes are crafted to maximize comedic payoff rather than to advance a thesis or political message that overrides structure or punch. Anti-patterns: didactic bits where the humor is sacrificed to make a point; substituting righteous indignation or moral argument for actual joke construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have you developed in alt rooms before chasing mainstream?
rubrics_metrics.description: Have you developed in alt rooms before chasing mainstream? Splitsider notes comics should develop in alt rooms before monetizing in mainstream rooms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a comic's trajectory and readiness: evidence of experimentation, stage-testing, and voice refinement in alt spaces suggests preparedness for larger, more commercial platforms. Anti-patterns: accelerating to mainstream showcases without sufficient development, which can result in thin, formulaic sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Are you the comic, or are you the comic's marketing?
rubrics_metrics.description: Are you the comic, or are you the comic's marketing? A criterion that asks whether a performer is prioritizing branding/marketable persona over comedic substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether material and performance choices are driven by authentic comedic goals or by creating shareable moments, headlines, or a marketable image. Anti-patterns: prioritizing viral one-liners, social-media-ready angles, or persona branding at the expense of layered joke construction and audience experience.
